families.t: system earthing, equipment earthing, bonding, liquid transfer, powder transfer, tanker offloading, flexible hoses and testing
f: System earthing supports correct operation, while equipment earthing protects people and plant.
Equipment earthing provides a controlled route for dissipating static electricity.
Flammable-liquid transfer can generate static charge through charge separation.
Contaminants, suspended solids or a second liquid phase can increase charging.
Conductive plant, flanges, hoses and transfer equipment should be bonded and earthed where required.
Low transfer velocities and bottom or subsurface filling can reduce electrostatic generation.
Powder conveying can charge both product and pipework and requires conductive, bonded equipment.
Earth bonds and hose continuity should be inspected and tested at suitable intervals.

families.s: HSE emergency isolation after loss of containment
families.t: remote valves, automatic isolation, manual isolation, depressurisation, diversion, release reduction, ALARP and detector integration
f: Emergency isolation is intended to limit releases after a breach of containment.
Strategically located isolation valves can reduce the quantity and duration of a release.
Alternatives can include depressurising, diverting or dumping material to a safer location.
The absence of isolation valves should be justified by equally effective risk-reduction measures.
Isolation can be manual, remotely operated or automatic.
Automatic or remote isolation may be initiated by pressure sensors, gas detectors or other instrumentation.
Selection should consider substance hazards, inventory, pressure, detection time, escalation and risk to personnel.
Emergency-isolation arrangements should be demonstrated as consistent with good practice and ALARP.

families.s: HSE emergency response and spill-control technical measures
families.t: loss of containment, on-site plan, incident control, people, environment, property, equipment, communications and recovery
f: Emergency response and spill control are fundamental elements of a process-safety management system.
Plant design and operating procedures should support credible emergency actions.
On-site plans should address loss-of-containment events.
Incident control should minimise effects and limit danger to people, the environment and property.
Plans should identify roles, communications, equipment and escalation arrangements.
Spill-control measures should reflect the substance, quantity, location and likely movement of a release.
Emergency equipment and procedures should be maintained, tested and exercised.
Lessons from drills and incidents should be used to improve arrangements.

families.s: HSE explosion-prevention and explosion-relief technical measures
families.t: prevention, vent panels, doors, ducting, rapid response, toxic releases, design basis, maintenance and consequence control
f: Explosion prevention is preferable to relying on explosion protection.
Operators should provide measures either to prevent explosions or minimise their effects.
Explosion relief is different from ordinary pressure relief because explosions develop very rapidly.
Explosion vents or doors may need large areas to relieve pressure fast enough.
Downstream ducting can restrict relief flow and must be designed carefully.
Relief discharge should not create unacceptable hazards to people or adjacent plant.
Explosion-relief design should reflect the material, enclosure, ignition scenario and credible pressure rise.
Relief devices and protected equipment require inspection, maintenance and management of changes.

families.s: HSE hazardous-area classification and ignition-source control
families.t: release sources, zones, gases, vapours, explosive atmospheres, equipment selection, documentation and DSEAR
f: DSEAR requires a hazardous-area study where explosive atmospheres may form.
The conclusions of the study should be documented as hazardous zones.
Classification starts by identifying normal and foreseeable sources of flammable-gas or vapour release.
Release frequency and duration influence the assigned zone.
Explosive atmospheres can also exist inside process equipment when fuel and air are present.
Electrical and non-electrical ignition sources should be systematically identified and controlled.
Equipment used in classified areas should be suitable for the zone and substance.
Area classifications should be reviewed when plant, materials, ventilation or operating conditions change.
